newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Police confirm death of Ethiopian hijackers.
newsitem.headline: Police confirm death of Ethiopian hijackers.

text.p: Police confirmed on Wednesday three men who hijacked an Ethiopian Airlines plane two weeks ago were Ethiopians and were killed when it crashed just off the Comoro Islands.
State-run Ethiopian Radio quoted police as saying the three Ethiopians lived in the Red Sea state of Djibouti for years before coming to Addis Ababa five weeks before the November 23 hijacking.
The radio identified them as Alamayhu Bekele, Mateias Solomon and Sultan Hussein and said they had lived in a rented house in the Ethiopian capital before hijacking flight ET 961.
It quoted police as saying the hijackers were not members of any political party and that their motive for commandeering the plane on a scheduled flight to Nairobi was to reach Australia.
It said they were not armed. It added the plane's "black box" flight recorder was found but had not yet been analysed.

Accounts by the two pilots and other survivors had painted a picture of three young men from the Horn of Africa with a strong grudge, a slender grasp of geography and finally a readiness to kill a plane-load of innocent people when their plan went awry.

In one of the deadliest acts in the history of air piracy, they seized the Boeing 767 on November 23 after take-off from Addis Ababa and kept control for nearly four hours before the pilot ditched into the Indian Ocean after it ran out of fuel.

The hijackers, who had demanded to be taken to Australia for political asylum and remained standing until the end, were presumed to have died in the crash which killed 125 of the 175 passengers and crew.
The dead included award-winning cameraman Mohamed Amin.

Survivors said the hijackers were in their mid-twenties, resembled Ethiopians or maybe Somalis, and did not move from the plane's cockpit and first-class cabin. They spoke to each other in French, which is one of Djibouti's official languages.

They threatened to blow the plane up with what they said was a bomb and said they had a problem with the government and had been prisoners. They were also armed with the plane's axe and a fire extinguisher.
Two passengers were detained by Comoran authorities for a week as suspected hijackers but were released on Saturday.

The bodies of 35 people who perished in the hijacking arrived in Addis Ababa from Comoros earlier on Wednesday. Seventeen other bodies had already been flown from the Indian Ocean archipelago to their respective countries.
On hand to receive the bodies in Addis Ababa were Ethiopian President Negasso Gidada, cabinet ministers and relatives.
Airline sources said the bodies of the remaining 73 dead would be flown to Addis Ababa and then flown to their home countries as soon as the identification process was completed in Comoros.
